title: Prime Data Centers — Technology Study Guide

sections.title: Start here: recapitalising a build-to-suit pipeline
ps: The Compass guide teaches how a pension fund and an infrastructure fund own a landlord and how the same building is paid for three times; the EdgeCore guide teaches the lease and the limited-recourse loan; the PowerHouse guide teaches the GP fund that puts in 10% of the equity. Each of those developers has one sponsor. This guide is about the one that does not: **a founder-owned developer that has been {{recapitalised}} five times without giving up control — a strategic partner, two institutional investors, a joint-control clearance, a joint-venture cheque, {{preferred equity}} at the parent — and that finances its buildings one lease at a time in the bond market when the corporate raise stalls.** Prime Data Centers is the worked example because its record is unusually legible for a private company: the European Commission's notice of who controls it, Bloomberg's account of the bond it priced and the bond it shelved, a plaintiffs' complaint that states the valuation, and location pages that list every building's status.

**Four things this guide teaches.** The {{recapitalisation ladder}} of a founder-owned developer — what each round buys and gives away, why 'majority founder-owned' and 'jointly controlled' can both be true, and what a preferred round at the parent means for the operating company. Project debt priced on a neocloud: how a 15-year CoreWeave lease supports USD 900 million of 7.5% notes, why that coupon is higher than Fleet's 5.9% on a AA- tenant, and why a Nordic bond for the pipeline failed the same summer. {{Phantom equity}} and the price of a founder-controlled cap table: what former executives say they were promised, what a 'two-tiered valuation' would mean, and how to read a USD 6 billion number that only the plaintiffs have stated. And utility pacing: how Oncor's 2023 push of 2 GW to 2027, SRP's deposit regime and ComEd's queue set the delivery dates a developer's capital cannot.

**What it deliberately leaves to other guides.** The lease itself (EdgeCore, Fluidstack); the sponsor's fund and ABS machinery (Compass); powered land and the utility contracts (PowerHouse, Tract); the neocloud's own balance sheet (CoreWeave dossier). Company history, executives and site lists stay in the dossier.

sections.title: The recapitalisation ladder: five rounds without losing the company
ps: A developer that owns its buildings needs equity roughly in proportion to its pipeline, and a founder who wants to keep control must raise it in forms that do not vote him out. Prime's five rounds are a catalogue of those forms. 2021: a {{strategic partner}} — Macquarie Capital's equity investment and a 'USD 5 billion over the next 10 years' capital plan, which buys a co-investor with deep pockets and a right to be consulted. 2023–2025: two 'existing institutional investors', Ares Management and Siemens Financial Services, added as the pipeline grew. Early 2025: {{joint control}} — the European Commission's clearance (Case M.11843) records that Ares acquired joint control 'through contractual means' alongside Macquarie and Data Realty Group, the founder's holding company. July 2025: a joint-venture cheque from Snowhawk and Nuveen during a reported USD 2 billion raise. April 2026: {{preferred equity}} from Grain Management into Data Realty Holding Corp. itself — money to the parent, not the company.

Two phrases have to be read together. 'Majority founder-owned' (the company's site) describes economic ownership; 'joint control' (the Commission's notice) describes who can block decisions. A founder can hold most of the shares and still need Macquarie's and Ares's consent for a budget, a sale or a new campus, because control in merger law means veto rights over strategic decisions, not a share count. The corpus's other developers are either sponsor-controlled outright (EdgeCore, Compass) or one-fund GP platforms (PowerHouse); Prime is the negotiated middle.

Preferred equity at the parent is the round that reveals the pressure. Preferred stock pays a fixed return ahead of common and converts or is redeemed on terms — cheaper than selling control, dearer than debt. Placing it in Data Realty Holding Corp. rather than in Prime means the founder's holding company borrowed against its stake to fund the operating company's plan without diluting the operating company's other investors; Grain's 'ability to provide additional capital over time' is an option on more of the same. The August 2026 suits name that parent as a defendant, which is why its cap table now matters to a bond buyer.

The failed raise is the missing rung. Infralogic reported in May 2025 that a roughly USD 2 billion equity raise run by Guggenheim and Moelis had slipped from the first quarter because of 'prolonged ongoing lease negotiations' — the capital would not come until the leases did. The pattern of 2025–2026 follows: sign CoreWeave, then sell a bond on the CoreWeave building; announce Snowhawk and Grain in the gaps; try a Nordic bond for the rest and withdraw it.

sections.title: Pricing a bond on a neocloud lease: 7.5% at Elk Grove, 5.9% at Fleet
ps: Elk Grove Village Property LLC — 'a wholly-owned indirect subsidiary of Prime Data Centers LLC' — priced USD 900 million of five-year {{senior secured notes}} at par with a 7.5% coupon on 2 June 2026, upsized from USD 850 million with Santander as sole bookrunner, to refinance USD 500 million of existing debt and 'fund the remaining estimated construction costs'. The security is the campus and the lease: CoreWeave's 15-year build-to-suit lease of the three Chicago buildings, worth about USD 2.2 billion with two seven-year renewals. This is the same instrument as Fleet's Storey County notes and the same season; the coupon is 160 basis points higher.

The spread is the tenant. Fleet's tenant is 'AA- … market cap in excess of USD 3 trillion'; Prime's is CoreWeave — a listed neocloud with tens of billions of its own debt, a business that depends on a few AI customers and a credit rating several notches below investment grade. A {{credit tenant lease}} to a AA- name lets a landlord borrow at nearly the tenant's cost of funds; a lease to a single-B neocloud carries the neocloud's risk into the landlord's bond. The Fluidstack guide teaches the tenant's side of that chain; Prime shows it from the landlord's — the campus is fully leased and the debt is still 7.5%.

Why the Nordic bond failed is the same lesson in reverse. A Norwegian-law high-yield bond is a fast, covenant-light way for a private company to raise USD 300–600 million from Nordic and international funds; Prime cut its planned USD 600 million to USD 500 million and then shelved it in July 2026 'after investors balked at the proposed terms'. The Elk Grove notes had a specific building, a specific lease and a specific tenant behind them; the Nordic bond would have funded a pipeline — Phoenix, Austin, the Nordics — with tenants unnamed. Bond buyers in 2026 would lend against a signed lease at 7.5% and would not lend against a roadmap at any price the company would pay.

Read the two together as the capital markets' rule for a mid-tier developer: project debt is available building by building once a lease is signed, priced on the tenant's credit; corporate debt for the pipeline is not. That is why the site says '4+ GW' and the bond says 270 MW.

sections.title: Phantom equity and the price of control: reading the employee suits
ps: {{Phantom equity}} is a promise of cash equal to what a share would be worth, without the share: a private company grants an executive units that pay out on a sale or a valuation event, so the employee shares the upside and the founder keeps the cap table clean. It is common in founder-controlled developers because real equity would dilute control and complicate every investor round. Its weakness is that the value is whatever the company says it is — the valuation is set by the party that pays.

That is the substance of the August 2026 suits. Seven former employees, among them the former Chief Commercial Officer, the former VP of Human Resources and the former Head of Utilities and Incentives, sued Prime, Data Realty Holdings and the two founders in Dallas County, the Southern District of New York and California for fraud, misrepresentation and civil RICO, claiming USD 185 million in Texas and 'more than USD 400 million' in total. Their allegations, as reported: a 'two-tiered valuation system' (one number for investors, one for employees), coerced re-signing of phantom-equity agreements, 'undisclosed property transactions absorbing co-owner interests' and dilution through 'unfunded paper commitments' — and a company valuation that went 'from about USD 140 million to more than USD 6 billion'. No defence had been reported by September 2026; allegations are not findings.

Two things matter to a reader who is not a party. First, the USD 6 billion is the only valuation on the public record and it comes from the plaintiffs — it should be quoted as their claim, not as the company's worth; the company's own scale claims moved from '4+ GW' to '7 GW' inside the same spring. Second, the plaintiffs are the commercial team that signed Lambda and negotiated with Oncor; a developer whose commercial leadership is litigating against it is a counterparty whose institutional memory of its own deals is in the courtroom.

For a supplier, the operative question is the same one the bond market asked: which entity signs, and what stands behind it. Elk Grove's bondholders have a lien on a building and a CoreWeave lease; a vendor to Avondale has a project company and an unnamed hyperscaler; a vendor to the parent has a defendant.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The pipeline number is a marketing figure.** '4+ GW' on the site and '7 GW' in the Grain release, in the same month, for a company operating 151 MW. Count buildings with a status field.

**Control and ownership are different sentences.** 'Majority founder-owned' and 'jointly controlled by Ares and Macquarie' are both true; a counterparty negotiating with the founder is negotiating with three vetoes.

**Project debt is not corporate capacity.** The Elk Grove notes financed one leased campus at 7.5%; the pipeline bond failed. Every unleased campus — Avondale's buildings 4–5, Austin, the Nordics — still needs the equity the 2025 raise did not deliver.
**The tenant sets the coupon.** A neocloud lease costs 160 basis points more than a AA- lease in the same market and season; 'fully leased' does not mean 'cheaply financed'.

**The commercial team is in court.** The executives who signed the leases and negotiated with Oncor are plaintiffs alleging a two-tiered valuation; the defendants include the parent that Grain just financed.

**Dates belong to the utility.** Oncor's 2027, SRP's deposits, a filed Fort Worth completion date with no opening, a Phoenix building whose first announced completion (Q3 2025) became a May 2026 groundbreaking.

cards.q: What does 'recapitalise' mean for a private developer?
cards.a: To change who funds the company and on what terms — new equity, preferred stock or debt — usually to fund growth or refinance, without necessarily changing who runs it.

cards.q: How can a company be 'majority founder-owned' and 'jointly controlled' by two investors at once?
cards.a: Ownership is a share count; control in merger law is veto rights over strategic decisions. A founder can hold most shares and still need Ares's and Macquarie's consent for a budget or a sale.

cards.q: What is preferred equity, and why put it in the parent rather than the company?
cards.a: Stock with a fixed return paid ahead of common. Placing it in Data Realty Holding Corp. funds the founder's stake without diluting the operating company's other investors — cheaper than selling control, dearer than debt.

cards.q: Why is the Elk Grove bond's coupon (7.5%) higher than Fleet's Nevada notes (5.875%)?
cards.a: The tenant: CoreWeave is a leveraged, sub-investment-grade neocloud; Fleet's tenant is AA-. Project bonds price on the lease counterparty's credit.

cards.q: What is a Norwegian-law bond, and why did Prime's fail?
cards.a: A fast, covenant-light Nordic high-yield instrument. Prime's would have funded an unleased pipeline; investors 'balked at the proposed terms' in July 2026 while the CoreWeave-backed notes had sold in June.
A cash promise equal to a share's value without the share — keeps the founder's cap table clean; its value is whatever the company's valuation says, which is the dispute in the 2026 suits.

cards.q: What is a 'two-tiered valuation system' as alleged?
cards.a: One valuation shown to investors and a lower one used to settle employees' phantom equity — the plaintiffs' allegation, not a finding.

cards.q: Why did a USD 2 billion equity raise slip in 2025?
cards.a: 'Prolonged ongoing lease negotiations' — investors wanted the leases before the equity, which is why the bond followed the CoreWeave signing rather than preceding it.

cards.q: What does a building's 'Operational / Leased' status field tell you that a pipeline figure does not?
cards.a: That a specific building exists and has a tenant — the only counter that reconciles with revenue; '4+ GW' and '7 GW' count plans.
Delivery dates set by the utility's ability to connect load — Oncor's push of 2 GW to 2027, SRP's deposit regime, ComEd's queue — which capital cannot shorten.

cards.q: Name the three things a supplier should identify before contracting with a founder-owned developer.
cards.a: Which entity signs (project company, operating company or parent), what stands behind it (a lease and a lien, an investor's consent, or a defendant), and whether the building has a status field or a pipeline claim.

cards.q: What did the EC's clearance of Case M.11843 establish?
cards.a: That Ares, Macquarie and Data Realty Group jointly control Prime — the only public record of the control structure.

glossary.d: The 'founding and controlling shareholder of Prime Data Centers' — the founder-controlled parent into which Grain Management made a preferred-equity investment in April 2026, and a defendant in the August 2026 employee suits.
The wholly owned Prime subsidiary that owns the Chicago campus leased to CoreWeave and issued USD 900 million of five-year 7.5% senior notes in June 2026.
